name: Potosí
info: Potosí is a city in the Andes of Bolivia, founded in 1545 as a mining town at the foot of the Cerro Rico, whose silver made it a Spanish imperial city, and now the capital of the Department of Potosí.

facts.founded: Founded in 1545 as a mining town after Diego Huallpa, an indigenous prospector, was traditionally credited with discovering the Cerro Rico in that year.
facts.where: At the foot of the Cerro de Potosí, or Cerro Rico, in the Andes of Bolivia, at a nominal 4,067 m above sea level.
facts.known: The Cerro Rico and its silver; the Spanish mint and the pieces of eight; the mita system of forced labour; the patio and pan amalgamation processes; the Villa Imperial of the Viceroyalty of Peru; the expression valer un Potosí; the colonial historic centre
facts.today: Potosí is the capital city of the Department of Potosí in Bolivia, a mining centre, and, with the Cerro Rico, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Potosí was founded in 1545 beside a mountain of silver and grew to a population that eventually exceeded 200,000.

The silver was won by Indigenous workers, many of them conscripted each year under the mita, who carried ore up shafts by candlelight, and many died or were seriously injured in the mines and the refining.
The easily smelted ore was exhausted by 1565, mercury amalgamation took its place, Guanajuato overtook the mountain in the 18th century, and from 1891 tin replaced silver as the main mineral.
dyk: The Cerro Rico produced an estimated 60% of all silver mined in the world during the second half of the 16th century, and a Spanish expression, valer un Potosí, still means to be worth a great deal.
ev: Founded as a mining town after the traditional discovery of the Cerro Rico
The ore that could be smelted directly is exhausted and silver production falls sharply
An anonymous description counts at least 120,000 native Andeans among the city's residents
The pan amalgamation process is invented in Potosí
Armed conflict between the Basque and Vicuña factions begins and lasts until 1625
The number of mitayos has dropped to about 4,000
The Bolivian War of Independence begins, and the city passes between Royalist and Patriot forces
Low silver prices bring a change to the mining of tin

sections.origins:
Potosí lies at the foot of the Cerro de Potosí, also called the Cerro Rico, the “rich mountain”, which is popularly conceived of as made of silver ore. The city stands at a nominal 4,067 m, and the peak of the mountain is 4,824 m above sea level. The ore lies in veins in a dacite volcanic dome that was extruded about 13.8 million years ago, and the hill is honeycombed with underground workings that reach from the summit to depths of 1,150 m. Diego Huallpa, an indigenous prospector, is traditionally credited with the discovery of the Cerro Rico in 1545, and the town was founded as a mining town in that year.

There is no authoritative etymology for the name. According to legend, the Sapa Inca Huayna Capac saw the hill on a journey from his mines at Ccolque Porco and Andaccaua, said that it must have much silver in its heart, and ordered his vassals to work it. They heard a thunderous noise and a voice that said the silver was destined for other masters, and the word they used for the noise, “Potocsí”, was said to have become the name. Potosí is believed to be a Quechua word, but in Quechua the root p’otoj does not refer to a thunderous noise, whereas in Aymara it does. Several Quechua speakers explain it instead as an onomatopoeic word for the sound of the hammer against the ore.
sections.growth:
The town produced great wealth quickly, and its population eventually exceeded 200,000. The miners at first worked rich oxidised ores containing native silver and silver chloride, which could be fed directly into smelting furnaces. Especially successful were small clay furnaces called guayras, which the Incas had used. By 1565 this ore was exhausted and production fell sharply. It recovered with the patio process, invented by the Spanish merchant Bartolomé de Medina in 1554, which used mercury amalgamation to extract silver from lower-grade ores, and from 1609 with the pan amalgamation process, invented in Potosí and better adapted to its conditions. At the peak of production in the 16th and 17th centuries the ore contained up to 40% silver.

The Spanish crown profited most. It let private entrepreneurs work mines under licence and taxed their profits heavily, among other levies by the quinto, a 20% severance tax on gross value. Coins called pieces of eight were struck at the Potosí mint. The silver went by llama and mule train to the Pacific coast, by ship to Panama City, across the isthmus by mule train to Nombre de Dios or Portobelo, and from there to Spain on the treasure fleets. Some went east to Buenos Aires, and some to Acapulco, from where the Manila galleons carried it to buy Asian goods. Guanajuato in Mexico surpassed Potosí as a source of silver in the 18th century.
sections.rulers:
Potosí lay in the Viceroyalty of Peru, in the region the Spanish called Upper Peru, and it was important enough to be designated a Villa Imperial in the hierarchy of Spanish urban settlements. Its core was laid out in the standard Spanish grid, while the rancherías, the Indigenous settlements on the northern flank of the Cerro Rico, were more haphazard. A Spanish corregidor, two alcaldes and a town council of 19 men governed it. The crown bureaucracy was a significant presence, five public scribes and some forty independent notaries recorded transactions and wills, and an ecclesiastical court heard cases concerning the clergy. The Inquisition had no tribunal in the city and relied on a commissioner.

In the early 17th century the Basques, who made up a substantial number of the inhabitants, formed a confederation opposed to the Vicuñas, a group of natives and non-Basque Spanish and Portuguese colonists, and the two fought for control of ore extraction and its management. Armed conflict lasted from 1622 to 1625. The crown intervened and at one point sided with the Basques, and the factions settled with a marriage between the children of their leaders.

During the Bolivian War of Independence (1809 to 1825) the city passed repeatedly between Royalist and Patriot forces. When the Second Auxiliary Army from Buenos Aires under Manuel Belgrano was forced to retreat, Belgrano decided to blow up the Casa de la Moneda, but the natives undid the fuse, since many people refused to leave and would have died. Two more expeditions from Buenos Aires took Potosí.
sections.life:
Indigenous workers were required to work in the mines under the Spanish mita system, based on a traditional Andean mit’a that had directed labour to public works and collective farming. Workers came from an area of almost 200,000 square miles, and thirteen thousand men were conscripted each year, about one in seven adult males of the Indigenous population. Skilled workers extracted the ore, while the mitayos carried it up in baskets, leather bags or cloth sacks. The loads often weighed 100 to 300 lbs, and the men climbed rickety ladders in steep, narrow shafts lit by a candle tied to the forehead. Many died or were seriously injured in falls and accidents. Pneumonia was a constant danger, as men climbed from the heat of the deep shafts to the cold at 16,000 feet, and mercury poisoning killed many in the refining.

Mine and mill owners notoriously ignored the rules on provisions and withheld travel money, and the cost of travelling to Potosí and back could exceed a mitayo’s pay for a year. Many stayed on as wage workers, and former mitayos, exempt from the draft, usually earned more. A 1603 report counted 58,800 Indians at work, of whom 5,100 were mitayos, 10,500 were mingas, or contract workers, and 43,200 were free wage earners. Noble David Cook takes this to show that mita labour was one form of work among several. Peter Bakewell stresses its role: as few as 4,500 mitayos worked at a time, because the up to 13,500 conscripted each year were divided in three, each part working one week in three, and many other workers were mitayos in their weeks off or former mitayos.
sections.crises:
The mita changed the region around it. Wives and children moved to Potosí with the workers, and thousands more fled their villages and gave up their ayllu land rights to escape the draft. The affected area stretched, in rough terms, from Quito to Buenos Aires. By the late 17th century Upper Peru had lost nearly 50% of its Indigenous population compared with a little over a century earlier. This increased the burden on those who remained, and at some point in the 1600s up to half of the eligible men might find themselves working at Potosí.

By 1689 the number of mitayos had fallen to about 4,000. The Viceroy, the Duke of Palata, tried to raise it again with a new census that included the forasteros, who were not subject to the mita. It is suspected that Spanish authorities in Arica, Chuquisaca and Oruro did not respond to calls from Potosí to find those who had escaped, since many had proved useful on the haciendas of influential Spaniards. The reform failed. The Duke’s successor set the official number at 4,108 mitayos, 1,367 of them active each week, and in practice it was lower still, because more and more men bought their way out of the obligation.

The ore itself failed too. The direct-smelting ore was exhausted by 1565, and the mountain was later overtaken by Guanajuato. In 1891 low silver prices prompted a change to mining tin, which continued until 1985.
sections.legacy:
Potosí gave Spanish a lasting expression, valer un Potosí, “to be worth a Potosí”, meaning to be of great value, and Miguel de Cervantes mentions it in the second part of Don Quixote as a land of extraordinary richness. One theory holds that the mint mark of Potosí, the letters PTSI superimposed on one another, is the origin of the dollar sign. The city of San Luis Potosí in Mexico was named after it, and so were the lead-mining towns of Potosi, Wisconsin, and Potosi, Missouri, and the silver-mining town of Potosi, Nevada.

The Cerro Rico is the world’s largest silver deposit, and it had produced up to 60,000 tonnes by 1996. Estimates are that much silver still remains in the mines. Workers in the mines have offered coca leaves and alcohol to statues of el Tío, a figure of the mountain itself, to protect them. A considerable amount of the colonial architecture has been preserved in the historic centre, and the centre and the Cerro Rico together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Large churches, lavishly decorated inside, were built in the colonial city, and no convent for women existed there until 1650.

Potosí is the capital of the Department of Potosí and its largest urban centre, and it continues to be an important mining centre. The Potosí Silversmithing School was established in 2011 as part of an industrialisation effort.

summary: Potosí, in the Bolivian Andes, was founded in 1545 at the foot of the Cerro Rico and became a Spanish imperial city of more than 200,000 people. Its silver was mined by Indigenous workers, many of them conscripted under the mita, at a heavy cost in lives. It is now the capital of its department.
references: Lewis Hanke, The Imperial City of Potosí (Nijhoff, 1956)
notes: Only the city's own article exists (no history article); every fact comes from it.
START: the article says the town was 'Founded in 1545' and that Diego Huallpa is 'traditionally credited' with the discovery in 1545; I used 1545 with circa false and kept the tradition attributed.

DEATHS: the article gives no count of deaths in the mines or mills, only that many died or were seriously injured and that mercury poisoning took the lives of many. I gave no figure. The article also says nothing about the number of enslaved Africans working in the mines, only that 5,000 Africans lived in the city in 1603 (I left that figure out for space).

The 1603 figures: the anonymous description (6,000 Spaniards and Europeans, 5,000 Africans, at least 120,000 native Andeans) and the 1603 report of 58,800 Indians at work are both in the article; I used the 120,000 in an event and the 58,800 breakdown in 'life'.
Cook and Bakewell disagree on how large the mita's role was; both are attributed and the article's reconciling detail (mita ordinaria, one week in three) is given.

Medina's patio process is dated 1554 in the article, before the 1565 exhaustion; I kept the article's order and did not say where it was invented. Huayna Capac's date of about 1462 is in the article but is evidently unreliable for the legend; I left the date out and kept the legend attributed.
The article says Potosí was the second largest city in the world after London 'at the turn of the 16th/17th centuries' and 'at this time' (1603); I wrote 'around 1600'.
'Eventually exceeded 200,000' has no year in the article. The 1603 count of residents (about 131,000 or more) is lower, so the two are not directly comparable.

Left out: the Catalina de Erauso passage, the sex workers and market women, the neighbourhood list, sports, airport and railway, climate, the Potosí 2011 school beyond one mention, and the geology of the Venus breccia.
Independence: the article names Castelli's First Auxiliary Army but gives no outcome beyond 'major leadership mistakes'; I left it out. It does not say when Potosí became part of Bolivia.
The legacy sentence about the colonial churches and the women's convent is placed there only because the article gives no better place; the convent fact could be moved to 'rulers'.
